Q: How to enqueue scripts properly in WordPress theme? A:

When you are learning WordPress theme development, one of the best habits you can build early is getting comfortable with the official WordPress documentation. The WordPress Codex and the newer Developer Resources explain very clearly how WordPress expects themes and plugins to work, and functions like wp_enqueue_script() and wp_enqueue_style() are a good example of that. Simply searching for those function names will usually take you straight to the official documentation, where the purpose, parameters, and common use cases are explained in detail.

Regarding script and style loading, while you may see examples online where <script> or <link> tags are placed directly inside header.php or footer.php, this is not how WordPress recommends doing it. WordPress provides a built-in system for handling assets, and that system exists for a reason. By using wp_enqueue_script() and wp_enqueue_style() inside functions.php, you are working with WordPress instead of around it.

One of the practical reasons this matters is portability. Themes rarely stay on a single domain forever. Sites get moved, domains change, multisite setups are used, or themes are shared or sold. Hardcoding URLs inside template files makes all of that fragile. When you use WordPress functions like get_template_directory_uri() or get_stylesheet_directory_uri(), WordPress always resolves the correct path automatically, which is exactly what the documentation recommends.

Another important point, which is clearly covered in the Codex, is dependency management. WordPress already registers many common libraries and allows themes and plugins to declare dependencies between scripts. When you enqueue scripts properly, WordPress makes sure they are loaded in the correct order and only once. This avoids conflicts with plugins and prevents issues such as loading jQuery multiple times or loading a script before its dependency exists.

A simple way to understand the difference is to look at a real example. Let’s say you want to use Fancybox in your theme.

wp_enqueue_script('fancybox', get_stylesheet_directory_uri().'/assets/js/fancybox.min.js',array('jquery')); vs <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@fancyapps/ui@6.1/dist/fancybox/fancybox.umd.js"></script>

By using wp_enqueue_script() you are telling WordPress several things at once. First, you are giving the script a unique handle called fancybox. This handle is how WordPress internally tracks the script and prevents it from being loaded more than once. Second, you are telling WordPress where the file lives, using get_stylesheet_directory_uri(), which means the path will always be correct no matter what domain the site is running on or whether the theme is reused elsewhere. Third, by passing jquery as a dependency, you are telling WordPress that this script must only be loaded after jQuery is available. If jQuery is already registered by WordPress or another plugin, it will not be loaded again.

At that point, WordPress takes over. It decides when the script should be printed, ensures dependencies are met, and outputs the <script> tag automatically when wp_head() or wp_footer() runs. Your theme stays clean, and WordPress stays in control.

Using direct/hardcoded <script> will load the file directly, but WordPress has no awareness of it at all. There is no handle, no dependency information, and no way for WordPress or plugins to know that Fancybox is already present. If another plugin also loads Fancybox or expects it to load after jQuery, you can easily run into conflicts or duplicate loading. You also lose control over load order and placement, because this script exists completely outside WordPress’s enqueue system.

This is why, even when using a CDN, WordPress still recommends enqueueing the script instead of hardcoding the tag. You could load the exact same CDN file using the WordPress system:

wp_enqueue_script('fancybox','https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@fancyapps/ui@6.1/dist/fancybox/fancybox.umd.js',array('jquery'));

Functionally, the browser ends up loading the same JavaScript file, but the difference is that WordPress now knows about it. It can manage dependencies, avoid duplicates, and integrate properly.

Q: Export tmap to docx A:

The simple approach is to save as .png or .svg (might be better) with tmap::tamp_save(), e.g.

plt = 
  tmap::tm_shape(World) +
  tmap::tm_polygons(fill = "HPI")

# just an example 
if (!dir.exists(file.path('workdir', 'output'))) 
  dir.create(file.path('workdir', 'output'))

tmap::tmap_save(tm = plt, 
                filename = file.path('workdir', 'output', 'plt.png'), 
                width = 1000, 
                height = 750, 
                dpi = 300)

tmap::tmap_save(tm = plt, 
                filename = file.path('workdir', 'output', 'plt.svg'), 
                width = 1000, 
                height = 750, 
                dpi = 300)

We can then add to a .docx-file via file browser.
